questions.q: A turntable rotates at 30 revolutions per minute. What is its angular speed?
questions.solution: 30 revolutions per minute is 0.50 revolutions per second. Each revolution is \(2\pi\) radians, so \(\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 0.50 = 3.1\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: A point on a wheel is 0.50 m from the axis. The wheel rotates at \(4.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\). What is the speed of the point?
questions.solution: \(v = \omega r = 4.0 \times 0.50 = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Dividing instead of multiplying (8.0) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A car travels at \(10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) around a bend of radius 20 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
questions.solution: \(a = \frac{v^{2}}{r} = \frac{10^{2}}{20} = 5.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}\). Forgetting to square the speed (0.50) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A ball of mass 0.20 kg is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.60 m at \(3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). What centripetal force acts on it?
questions.solution: \(F = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} = \frac{0.20 \times 3.0^{2}}{0.60}\) = 3.0 N. Forgetting to square the speed (1.0 N) is the usual slip.

questions.q: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. In which direction does the resultant force on it act?

options.B: Opposite to the direction of motion.
options.C: Away from the centre of the circle.
options.D: Towards the centre of the circle.

questions.solution: The velocity keeps changing direction, so the object is accelerating, and the acceleration is towards the centre. By Newton's second law the resultant force is in the same direction: towards the centre. There is no outward force on the object.

questions.q: Why does the centripetal force on an object in uniform circular motion not change its speed?

options.A: It acts at right angles to the velocity, so it does no work.
options.B: It is balanced by an equal outward force.
options.C: It is too small to affect the speed.
options.D: It acts for too short a time.

questions.solution: Work is done only by the component of a force along the direction of motion. The centripetal force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the kinetic energy stays constant. It changes the direction of the velocity, not its size.

questions.q: A bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius 2.5 m. What is the minimum speed at the top of the circle for the water to stay in the bucket? (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: At the minimum speed the weight alone provides the centripetal force at the top: \(mg = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}\). So \(v = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{9.81 \times 2.5} = 5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: What is an angle of 90° in radians?
questions.solution: A full circle of 360° is \(2\pi\) rad, so 90° is a quarter of that: \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) = 1.57 rad.

questions.q: An object moves in a circle with an angular speed of \(5.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\). How long does one revolution take?
questions.solution: \(T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{5.0}\) = 1.3 s. Leaving out the \(2\pi\) (0.20 s) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A car goes round a bend on a flat, level road at constant speed. What provides the centripetal force?

options.B: The normal contact force from the road.
options.C: The driving force of the engine.
options.D: Friction between the tyres and the road.

questions.solution: On a level road the only horizontal force that can act towards the centre of the bend is the sideways friction between the tyres and the road. Weight and the normal contact force are vertical. This is why cars skid outwards on ice.

questions.q: A force of 200 N acts on a ball for 0.050 s. What is the impulse on the ball?
questions.solution: Impulse is force multiplied by the time it acts for, and equals the change in momentum: \(F\Delta t\) = 200 × 0.050 = 10 N s.

questions.q: A trolley of mass 2.0 kg has a momentum of \(6.0\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\). What is its kinetic energy?
questions.solution: For a non-relativistic particle, \(E_{k} = \frac{p^{2}}{2m} = \frac{6.0^{2}}{2 \times 2.0}\) = 9.0 J. Leaving out the 2 (18 J) is the usual slip.

questions.q: What is true of an elastic collision between two objects, with no external forces?

options.A: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.
options.B: Kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not.
options.D: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.

questions.solution: Momentum is conserved in every collision with no external forces. A collision is elastic only if the total kinetic energy is also the same before and after. If kinetic energy is lost, it is inelastic.

questions.q: A stationary object explodes into two pieces that fly apart across a smooth table. Which statement about the pieces is correct?

options.C: They move at right angles to each other.
options.D: Their momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction.

questions.solution: The total momentum was zero before the explosion, so it must be zero afterwards. In two dimensions that means the momentum vectors of the two pieces are equal in size and exactly opposite. Their speeds are equal only if their masses are.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg trolley moving east at \(3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) collides with a 2.0 kg trolley moving north at \(4.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). They stick together. What is their speed after the collision?
questions.solution: Momentum is conserved in each direction. East: 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0; north: 2.0 × 4.0 = 8.0. Total: \(\sqrt{6.0^{2} + 8.0^{2}} = 10\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\). The combined mass is 4.0 kg, so \(v = \frac{10}{4.0} = 2.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).
